Task: Feature Design & Build from a Vague Brief
Scenario
A product manager has handed you the following brief — exactly as written, nothing more:
"We want users to be able to set up alerts so they get notified when something important happens in the world — like breaking news, market movements, natural disasters, that kind of thing. Should work for both email and Slack. Make it flexible enough that we can add more channels later. We need an admin view too."
You may use any technology, language, or framework you choose.
There is no further specification. No wireframes. No schema proposal. No agreement on what "something important" means, where the data comes from, or how events are detected.
Your Task
Using AI agents, take this brief from ambiguity to a working implementation.
Before you start building, define your own plan of attack. Decide what deliverables you think this brief requires, what order to tackle them in, and why. Your plan is itself part of the evaluation — we want to see how you scope and structure work, not just how you execute a predefined checklist.
Then execute against your own plan. As you go, critically assess what the AI produces: don't assume outputs are correct just because they look plausible. Surface the checks you run, the things you reject, and the course-corrections you make — that judgment is as important as the work itself.
Suggested Timeframe
Plan for 24 hours. A partial but well-reasoned solution beats a complete but undocumented one — use the time to think, plan, and show your work, not to maximize output.
A Note on What We're Evaluating
We are not evaluating the solution itself. We are evaluating how you arrived at it.
A working, polished implementation with no visible process tells us very little. What we want to see is how you directed the AI: how you framed the problem, what decisions you made and why, where you course-corrected, and how you validated output before accepting it. The artifacts of that process — plans, decision logs, prompt drafts, notes, intermediate outputs — are the submission. The code is evidence, not the point.
We pay particular attention to how you evaluated the validity of what the AI produced — the assumptions you challenged, the hallucinations or shortcuts you caught, the code you rewrote or rejected, and the sanity checks you applied to generated artifacts.
AI Tooling
Use any AI tool(s) you prefer — there is no required or favored product.
What to Submit
Please share your results with us via a GitHub repository that must contain:
commits for each major milestone, with meaningful commit messages
your prompt history — all prompts used during the process
your plans, working artifacts, and evidence of how you worked — design docs, decision logs, prompt drafts, intermediate outputs, notes, scratch files, screenshots, etc.
your deliverables — as defined by your own plan

# Plan

## 1. How I read the brief

- **"Something important"** means an event that matches one of the user's rules and meets that rule's minimum severity.
- **Event categories:** `news`, `market`, `disaster`. Each has its own filters:
  - news: keywords
  - market: symbol, direction, minimum % change
  - disaster: type, region, minimum magnitude
- **Event data:** a generator in the backend creates fake events, one generator per category. Adding a real source later only needs a new class that implements the same interface.
- **Channels:** a `NotificationChannel` interface with a registry. Adding a new channel such as SMS means one new class plus a config schema.

## 2. Files to submit (the reviewers grade these)

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `docs/plan.md` | This plan, the order of work, what gets cut first |
| `docs/requirements.md` | How I interpreted the brief, assumptions, what is out of scope |
| `docs/design.md` | Data model, flow diagram, channel interface, API list |
| `docs/decision-log.md` | Each decision with the options considered and why |

|

| Run instructions, demo steps, screenshots |

## 3. Design

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[Event generators] --> E[(events)]
  E --> M[Matcher]
  M -->|insert, skip if exists| D[(deliveries)]
  D --> W[Delivery worker]
  W --> C{Channel registry}
  C --> Email[Email via Mailpit]
  C --> Slack[Slack webhook]
```

- **Database tables:**
  - `users`: includes a role, user or admin
  - `notification_targets`: user, channel type, config as JSON
  - `alerts`: category, filters as JSON, minimum severity, target ids
  - `events`
  - `deliveries`: status, attempts, next attempt time, last error. A unique key on (alert, event, target) stops the same notification from being sent twice.
  - `sources` and `channels`: on/off switches for the admin.
- **Queue:** the `deliveries` table is also the job queue. The worker claims jobs with Postgres `SKIP LOCKED`. On failure it waits twice as long before each retry, up to 5 attempts, then marks the delivery as dead. I chose this over the pg-boss library because the admin delivery log can then read and retry the same rows directly.
- **API (Fastify):**
  - Login and registration
  - Create, edit and delete alerts and notification targets
  - A "send test notification" action
  - Admin endpoints: users, events, deliveries with retry, sources and channels on/off, metrics
  - A dev-only endpoint to inject an event, so the e2e test and the demo give predictable results
- **Web app (Angular 22 with spartan-ng):**
  - Login
  - My alerts, with filter fields that change by category
  - My channels
  - Admin pages: users and alerts, events, deliveries, sources and channels, metrics

## 4. Milestones (one commit each, about 145 minutes in total)

| # | Milestone | Time | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0 | Process docs: plan, requirements, decision log, prompt log | 10 min | Files committed |
| M1 | Design doc | 15 min | Data model and API list reviewed by you |
| M2 | Nx workspace, Docker Compose, shared library | 15 min | `nx build` passes and containers start |
| M3 | Backend: schema, seed data, login, CRUD, generators, matcher, worker, both channels, unit tests | 40 min | An injected event produces a Mailpit email and a Slack message |
| M4 | Frontend: user pages and admin pages | 35 min | Manual demo works start to finish |
| M5 | API integration tests and one Playwright smoke test | 15 min | Tests pass |
| M6 | README, screenshots, final AI review log, chat export | 15 min | Submission is ready |

**Order:** docs come first because they are what gets graded and they shape every later prompt. The backend comes before the frontend because matching and delivery carry the most risk. The UI is built once the API is stable.

**If we fall behind:** cut, in this order, the metrics page, the Playwright test, then the source and channel switches. The process docs are never cut.

## Questions before I start

1. **Scope:** 2.5 hours leaves almost no slack for this scope. Do you accept the cut order above?
2. **Slack:** do you have a Slack workspace where you can create an incoming webhook? If not, I'll add a mock webhook receiver so the demo and tests still work.
3. **Commits:** should I commit at each milestone, with you doing all the pushes?
4. **Generated events:** should they appear on a timer, for example every 20 to 60 seconds per category, in addition to the dev injection endpoint?

Once you approve, I'll start M0, including logging your prompts so far word for word.

I checked your stack choices before planning:

- **Angular 22 and Nx:** `@nx/angular` 24.0.7 supports Angular versions below 23, so Angular 22 works.
- **shadcn-ui:** the Angular version is called spartan-ng. Version 1.10.1 supports Angular 21 and 22 and uses Tailwind 4, so we can use it. Angular Material stays the fallback.
- **Docker:** it is not installed yet. Once you install it, Docker Compose will run Postgres 18 and Mailpit, a local email server with a web inbox.

# Plan

## 1. How I read the brief

- **"Something important"** means an event that matches one of the user's rules and meets that rule's minimum severity.
- **Event categories:** `news`, `market`, `disaster`. Each has its own filters:
  - news: keywords
  - market: symbol, direction, minimum % change
  - disaster: type, region, minimum magnitude
- **Event data:** a generator in the backend creates fake events, one generator per category. Adding a real source later only needs a new class that implements the same interface.
- **Channels:** a `NotificationChannel` interface with a registry. Adding a new channel such as SMS means one new class plus a config schema.

## 2. Files to submit (the reviewers grade these)

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `docs/plan.md` | This plan, the order of work, what gets cut first |
| `docs/requirements.md` | How I interpreted the brief, assumptions, what is out of scope |
| `docs/design.md` | Data model, flow diagram, channel interface, API list |
| `docs/decision-log.md` | Each decision with the options considered and why |
| `docs/ai-review-log.md` | What the AI produced, how I checked it, what I rejected or fixed |
| `prompts/prompt-log.md` | Your prompts word for word, plus chat exports in `prompts/exports/` |
| Code | `apps/web`, `apps/api`, `libs/shared`, `docker-compose.yml` |
| `README.md` | Run instructions, demo steps, screenshots |

The AI review log already has two entries: the version checks above, and the plan change after finding Docker missing.

## 3. Design

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[Event generators] --> E[(events)]
  E --> M[Matcher]
  M -->|insert, skip if exists| D[(deliveries)]
  D --> W[Delivery worker]
  W --> C{Channel registry}
  C --> Email[Email via Mailpit]
  C --> Slack[Slack webhook]
```

- **Database tables:**
  - `users`: includes a role, user or admin
  - `notification_targets`: user, channel type, config as JSON
  - `alerts`: category, filters as JSON, minimum severity, target ids
  - `events`
  - `deliveries`: status, attempts, next attempt time, last error. A unique key on (alert, event, target) stops the same notification from being sent twice.
  - `sources` and `channels`: on/off switches for the admin.
- **Queue:** the `deliveries` table is also the job queue. The worker claims jobs with Postgres `SKIP LOCKED`. On failure it waits twice as long before each retry, up to 5 attempts, then marks the delivery as dead. I chose this over the pg-boss library because the admin delivery log can then read and retry the same rows directly.
- **API (Fastify):**
  - Login and registration
  - Create, edit and delete alerts and notification targets
  - A "send test notification" action
  - Admin endpoints: users, events, deliveries with retry, sources and channels on/off, metrics
  - A dev-only endpoint to inject an event, so the e2e test and the demo give predictable results
- **Web app (Angular 22 with spartan-ng):**
  - Login
  - My alerts, with filter fields that change by category
  - My channels
  - Admin pages: users and alerts, events, deliveries, sources and channels, metrics

## 4. Milestones (one commit each, about 145 minutes in total)

| # | Milestone | Time | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0 | Process docs: plan, requirements, decision log, prompt log | 10 min | Files committed |
| M1 | Design doc | 15 min | Data model and API list reviewed by you |
| M2 | Nx workspace, Docker Compose, shared library | 15 min | `nx build` passes and containers start |
| M3 | Backend: schema, seed data, login, CRUD, generators, matcher, worker, both channels, unit tests | 40 min | An injected event produces a Mailpit email and a Slack message |
| M4 | Frontend: user pages and admin pages | 35 min | Manual demo works start to finish |
| M5 | API integration tests and one Playwright smoke test | 15 min | Tests pass |
| M6 | README, screenshots, final AI review log, chat export | 15 min | Submission is ready |

**Order:** docs come first because they are what gets graded and they shape every later prompt. The backend comes before the frontend because matching and delivery carry the most risk. The UI is built once the API is stable.

**If we fall behind:** cut, in this order, the metrics page, the Playwright test, then the source and channel switches. The process docs are never cut.

1. **Scope:** 2.5 hours leaves almost no slack for this scope. Do you accept the cut order above?
2. **Slack:** do you have a Slack workspace where you can create an incoming webhook? If not, I'll add a mock webhook receiver so the demo and tests still work.

3. No trailing "-ing" phrases that add no fact ("highlighting...", "ensuring...").

11. One name per thing. Repeat it.
12. No "from X to Y" unless X and Y sit on a real scale.
13. No em dashes, en dashes, or hyphens used as dashes, and no parentheses in their place. Use a period or a comma.
14. A colon goes before a list or an example, never mid-sentence as a connector.
15. Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. No bold label and colon that restates its line ("**Performance:** Performance improved..."). A bold lead-in that ends in a period and adds new detail is fine.
20. No chatbot phrases ("I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...").
22. No praise or agreement openers. Respond directly.
23. Cut filler. "In order to" becomes "to". Delete "it is important to note that".
25. No generic conclusions. State specific plans or facts.
26. No abstract metaphor nouns: substrate, wedge, vector, nexus, primitive, harness, surface, scaffolding, paradigm, ratchet, north star, flywheel. Use the concrete word.
27. Say what it does, not how it feels. Name the mechanism or the number. Cut a sentence that could appear unchanged in another project's docs.
28. One idea per sentence. Split a sentence the reader has to reread.
29. Active voice. Name the actor unless it is unknown or doesn't matter.
30. Cut adverbs or use a stronger verb. Give the number.
31. Use the plain word: "use", not "utilize" or "leverage".
32. No metaphor, aphorism, personified code, or figurative verb where a literal phrase exists.
33. Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs. Spell out arrows and abbreviations.

# AGENTS.md

Instructions for every AI agent working in this repository.

## Project

An alerting app. Users create alert rules for world events in three categories: news, market and disaster. When an event matches a rule, the app notifies the user by email or Slack. Admins see all users, alerts, events and deliveries.

The repository is an interview submission. Reviewers grade the process, so the process artifacts matter as much as the code.

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/plan.md` | Milestones, order, cut list |
| `docs/requirements.md` | How the brief was interpreted, assumptions, out of scope |
| `docs/design.md` | Architecture, data model, API |
| `docs/decision-log.md` | Decisions with options and reasons |
| `docs/ai-review-log.md` | AI output that was checked, rejected or corrected |
| `prompts/prompt-log.md` | User prompts, word for word |
| `prompts/subagents/` | Prompts the orchestrator sent to subagents |

Read `docs/requirements.md` and `docs/design.md` before changing code.

## Stack

- Node.js 26 LTS, TypeScript, npm
- Nx 24 monorepo: `apps/api`, `apps/web`, `libs/shared`
- Backend: Fastify 5, Drizzle ORM, PostgreSQL 18
- Frontend: Angular 22, spartan-ng with Tailwind 4
- Email: Nodemailer to Mailpit. Slack: incoming webhook, with a mock receiver in development
- Docker Compose runs Postgres and Mailpit

## Agent roles

| Role | Who | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | Main chat agent | Plans, writes subagent prompts, verifies output, reconciles reviews, commits |
| Implementer | Default subagent | Writes code for one scoped task from a saved prompt |
| Explorer | `Explore` subagent | Read-only lookups |
| Reviewer A | `reviewer-opus` on Claude Opus 5.5 | Independent read-only review |
| Reviewer B | `reviewer-gpt` on GPT-6.2 Sol | Independent read-only review |

The two reviewer files in `.github/agents/` share the same body. Only the model differs. Keep the bodies identical so the reviews are comparable.

## Milestone workflow

1. The orchestrator saves the subagent prompt to `prompts/subagents/NNN-<slug>.md` before sending it.
2. An implementer subagent does the task.
3. The orchestrator checks the result itself: reads the diff, runs build and tests, and checks package versions with `npm view`.
4. Both reviewers get the same review prompt and run in parallel.
5. The orchestrator compares the two reviews. It accepts, rejects or defers each finding and records the outcome with a reason in `docs/ai-review-log.md`.
6. The orchestrator commits. The user pushes. Agents never push.

## Commit messages

Follow the [Angular commit message guidelines](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/contributing-docs/commit-message-guidelines.md).

```text
<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

<body>

<footer>
```

- Type is one of `build`, `ci`, `docs`, `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `refactor`, `test`.
- Scope is optional. Use `api`, `web`, `shared`, `e2e` or `infra`. Leave the scope empty for repository-wide docs.
- Write the summary in the imperative present tense, start it with a lowercase letter, and leave out the final period.
- Every commit except `docs` needs a body of at least 20 characters that explains why.

## Writing rules

Apply `.agents/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` to all prose in `docs/`, `prompts/`, `README.md` and this file.

## Code rules

- Keep secrets out of git. Put defaults in `.env.example`.
- The API rejects Slack webhook URLs whose host is not on the allowlist in `SLACK_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS`.
- Routes under `/dev` are registered only when `NODE_ENV` is not `production`.
- Validate every request body with the zod schemas in `libs/shared`.

# Plan

## Goal

Turn a one-paragraph product brief into a working alerting app and record how the work was done. The graders read the process artifacts first and use the code as evidence for them.

## Constraints

- About 2.5 hours on day one. The user may continue on day two.
- One developer directs AI agents. The orchestrator agent delegates implementation to subagents and sends every milestone to two reviewer agents on different models.
- Local run only.

## Deliverables

| Deliverable | Path | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | `docs/plan.md` | Shows scope, order and the cut list |
| Requirements | `docs/requirements.md` | Turns the vague brief into testable statements and lists assumptions |
| Design | `docs/design.md` | Fixes the data model and API before any code, so subagents share one contract |
| Decision log | `docs/decision-log.md` | Records each choice with the options and the reason |
| AI review log | `docs/ai-review-log.md` | Records what AI output was checked, rejected or corrected |
| Prompt history | `prompts/` | User prompts word for word, subagent prompts, chat exports |
| Agent setup | `AGENTS.md`, `.github/agents/` | Shows how the agents were directed |
| Code | `apps/`, `libs/`, `docker-compose.yml` | Evidence that the design works |
| README | `README.md` | Run instructions, demo script, screenshots |

## Milestones

Each milestone ends with a commit that follows the Angular convention in `AGENTS.md`.

| ID | Milestone | Budget | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0 | Process docs, agent setup, prompt log | 10 min | Files committed |
| M1 | Design doc, reviewed by both reviewer agents | 15 min | The user approves the data model and API list |
| M2 | Nx workspace, Docker Compose, shared library | 15 min | `nx run-many -t build` passes and the containers start |
| M3 | Backend: schema, seed, auth, CRUD, generators, matcher, worker, both channels, unit tests | 40 min | An injected event produces an email in Mailpit and a message in the mock Slack receiver |
| M4 | Frontend: user pages and admin pages | 35 min | The demo script in the README works by hand |
| M5 | API integration tests and one Playwright smoke test | 15 min | All tests pass |
| M6 | README, screenshots, final review log, chat export | 15 min | Submission is ready to push |

## Order and reasons

1. Process docs come first. The graders read them first, and every later subagent prompt points at them.
2. The design comes before code. Implementer subagents run in isolated contexts, so the design doc is the only contract they share.
3. The backend comes before the frontend. Matching, dedup and retries carry the most risk, and the UI only displays their results.
4. Tests run alongside the backend work. The matcher and the retry timing get unit tests in M3, and M5 adds the integration tests and the end-to-end test.

## Cut list

If a milestone runs over budget, features are cut in this order:

1. Metrics page
2. Playwright smoke test
3. Admin switches for sources and channels

The process docs are never cut.

## Day two candidates

These items are out of scope for day one. They come back if time allows:

- Rate limiting and digest batching
- Quiet hours
- A real event source, such as the USGS earthquake feed
- A third channel to prove the extension point

# Requirements

## The brief

> We want users to be able to set up alerts so they get notified when something important happens in the world, like breaking news, market movements, natural disasters, that kind of thing. Should work for both email and Slack. Make it flexible enough that we can add more channels later. We need an admin view too.

No product manager is available, so the user acts as the product owner. Answers are in `prompts/prompt-log.md`, entries 002 and 003.

## Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Event | One thing that happened in the world, such as an earthquake or a 7% drop in a stock price. It has a category, a severity from 1 to 5, and category-specific data. |
| Category | `news`, `market` or `disaster` |
| Source | A component that produces events for one category. On day one, every source is a simulator. |
| Alert | A rule owned by a user: a category, typed filters, a minimum severity, and one or more targets |
| Target | A destination owned by a user, such as an email address or a Slack webhook URL |
| Channel | A delivery mechanism, `email` or `slack`. Each target uses one channel. |
| Delivery | One attempt record for sending one event to one target because of one alert |

"Something important" means an event that matches an alert's filters and has a severity at or above the alert's minimum severity.

## Functional requirements

### Users

- R1. A visitor can register and sign in with an email address and a password.
- R2. A user can create, list and delete targets. An email target has an address. A Slack target has an incoming webhook URL.
- R3. A user can send a test notification to a target.
- R4. A user can create, edit, delete, enable and disable alerts.
- R5. Alert filters depend on the category:
  - news: keywords matched against the title and summary, case-insensitive, any keyword matches
  - market: symbols (an empty list means any symbol), direction (`up`, `down`, `any`), minimum absolute change in percent
  - disaster: types (`earthquake`, `flood`, `storm`, `wildfire`; an empty list means any type), regions (an empty list means any region), minimum magnitude for earthquakes
- R6. Every alert has a minimum severity from 1 to 5.

### System

- R7. Each enabled source produces one event at a random interval between 20 and 60 seconds.
- R8. When an event is stored, the system evaluates it against every enabled alert in the same category.
- R9. For each match, the system creates one delivery per target. The same alert, event and target never produce a second delivery.
- R10. A worker sends pending deliveries. A failed send is retried with exponential backoff, up to 5 attempts in total. After the fifth failure the delivery is marked `dead`.
- R11. If an admin has disabled a channel, new deliveries for that channel are stored with status `skipped`, so the admin can see why nothing was sent.

### Admin

- R12. An admin can list all users and the alerts each user owns.
- R13. An admin can browse stored events and filter them by category.
- R14. An admin can browse deliveries, filter them by status and channel, and retry a `failed` or `dead` delivery.
- R15. An admin can enable and disable each source and each channel.
- R16. An admin can see metrics for the last 24 hours: events per category, deliveries per status, and failure rate per channel.

### Development and demo

- R17. A route that exists only outside production lets a developer inject a specific event. Tests and demos use it to get predictable results.
- R18. A mock Slack receiver records incoming webhook calls and can be set to fail, so retries can be shown without a Slack workspace.

## Non-functional requirements

- N1. One command starts the stack locally after `docker compose up -d`. A seed script creates one admin and one demo user.
- N2. Passwords are stored as salted hashes. Admin routes check the role on the server.
- N3. Adding a channel needs one new module that implements the channel interface, one config schema, and one registry entry. The same applies to adding a source.
- N4. Slack webhook URLs must use HTTPS and a host from an allowlist. Development adds the mock receiver's host to the allowlist.
- N5. Unit tests cover filter matching, severity checks and backoff timing. Integration tests cover the API. One Playwright test covers sign-in, alert creation and delivery.

## Assumptions

- A1. Simulated events are enough to show the design. Real sources plug into the same source interface later.
- A2. A single API process runs the generators and the worker. The worker claims rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so a second process would not send twice.
- A3. All times are stored in UTC.
- A4. The UI is in English.

## Out of scope for day one

- Real data sources
- Rate limiting, digest batching and quiet hours
- Email verification and password reset
- Channels other than email and Slack
- Organisations or teams
- Deployment

# Decision log

Each entry records what was decided, which options were considered, who decided, and why. "User" means the user acting as product owner. "Orchestrator" means the main agent, with the user's approval of the plan.

## D-001 Event data is simulated

- Options: free public APIs with a simulator for demos, simulator only, public APIs only.
- Decided by: user.
- Reason: demos give the same result every time, no API keys are needed, and the time budget is 2.5 hours.
- Consequence: sources implement one interface, so a real feed such as USGS can replace a simulator without changes elsewhere.

## D-002 Alerts use category plus typed filters

- Options: category subscription only, category with typed filters, generic field and operator builder.
- Decided by: user.
- Reason: typed filters let a user express "earthquakes above magnitude 6 in Asia" without the cost of a query builder.

## D-003 Email and password sign-in with JWT and a seeded admin

- Options: email and password with JWT, fake user switcher, OAuth.
- Decided by: user.

## D-004 Docker Compose runs PostgreSQL 18 and Mailpit

- Options: SQLite, PostgreSQL.
- Decided by: orchestrator, after the user agreed to install Docker and asked for the best option.
- Reason: Postgres gives `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` for the delivery queue and `jsonb` for alert filters. Mailpit catches all SMTP mail and shows it in a web inbox, so no real mail leaves the machine.

## D-005 The deliveries table is the job queue

- Options: pg-boss, Redis with BullMQ, a `deliveries` table polled by a worker.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: the admin delivery log and the retry button read and update the same rows the worker uses. pg-boss stores jobs in its own schema, so the app would have to copy job state into a second table. Redis adds a service the app does not otherwise need.
- Consequence: dedup is a unique index on (alert, event, target), and retry timing is a `next_attempt_at` column.

## D-006 Slack uses incoming webhooks and a mock receiver

- Options: incoming webhook per target, Slack app with a bot token, mock only.
- Decided by: user chose incoming webhooks. The user has no Slack workspace, so the orchestrator added a mock receiver.
- Reason: a webhook URL is the smallest real Slack integration. The mock receiver can be set to fail, which shows retries in the demo.
- Consequence: the API sends HTTP requests to URLs that users type in, which is a server-side request forgery risk. The API accepts only HTTPS URLs on allowlisted hosts (requirement N4).

## D-007 Fastify for the API

- Options: NestJS, Fastify, Express.
- Decided by: user.

## D-008 Nx monorepo

- Options: npm workspaces, Nx, two separate folders.
- Decided by: user.
- Check: `npm view @nx/angular peerDependencies` shows Nx 24.0.7 accepts Angular versions from 20 up to, but not including, 23. Angular 22.3.0 fits.

## D-009 spartan-ng for UI components

- Options: Angular Material, PrimeNG, Tailwind only, plain CSS. The user asked for shadcn-ui with Angular Material as the fallback.
- Decided by: user.
- Check: shadcn-ui is a React library. Its Angular port is spartan-ng. `npm view @spartan-ng/brain peerDependencies` shows version 1.10.1 accepts Angular from 21 up to, but not including, 23, and needs Tailwind 4.

## D-010 Drizzle ORM

- Options: Prisma, Drizzle, raw `pg` queries.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: Drizzle defines the schema in TypeScript and has no code generation step or separate engine binary. Its query builder stays close to SQL, which makes the `SKIP LOCKED` claim query simple to write and to review.

## D-011 Angular commit message convention

- Decided by: user.
- Note: the Angular type list has no `chore` type. The earlier commit `chore: add gitignore and unslop skill` does not follow the convention. It is already pushed, so it stays as it is. Rewriting pushed history would need a force push.

## D-012 One orchestrator and two reviewers on different models

- Decided by: user.
- Setup: `reviewer-opus` runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and `reviewer-gpt` runs on GPT-6.2 Sol. Both agent files have the same body, so differences in the reviews come from the model and not from the instructions.
- Reason: the two models fail in different ways. Findings that only one reviewer reports get a second look from the orchestrator before they are accepted.

## D-013 Simulated events on a timer, plus an injection route

- Decided by: user.
- Setup: each source emits an event every 20 to 60 seconds. A route that exists only outside production injects a given event for tests and demos.

## D-014 Cut order

- Decided by: user accepted the orchestrator's proposal.
- Order: metrics page, then the Playwright test, then the admin switches for sources and channels.

# AI review log

This log records each AI output or claim that was checked before it was accepted, and the result of the check. Entries are in time order.

Status values: `accepted`, `corrected`, `rejected`, `open`.

## V-001 Reading the brief

- AI output: the first attempt to read the `.docx` file called `unzip`, which is not installed.
- Check: read the file with Python `zipfile`. Also opened `word/comments.xml`, `footnotes.xml` and `endnotes.xml` to look for hidden reviewer comments.
- Result: the brief has no comments, footnotes or endnotes. The plan is based only on the document body.
- Status: corrected.

## V-002 Angular 22 support in Nx and spartan-ng

- AI claim: Nx and spartan-ng work with Angular 22.
- Check: `npm view @nx/angular peerDependencies` and `npm view @spartan-ng/brain peerDependencies`.
- Result: Nx 24.0.7 accepts Angular versions from 20 up to, but not including, 23. spartan-ng 1.10.1 accepts versions from 21 up to, but not including, 23. Both fit Angular 22.3.0.
- Status: accepted.

## V-003 Local tooling

- AI plan: the first plan assumed Docker for Postgres and Mailpit.
- Check: `docker --version`.
- Result: Docker was not installed. The questions to the user were changed to offer options without Docker. The user then chose to install Docker.
- Status: corrected.

## V-004 Reviewer model names

- User input: "one Opus 5.5 agent, one GPT 6.2 Sol".
- Check: searched the local Copilot Chat storage for registered model names.
- Result: the registered names are `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6.2 Sol`, with a hyphen. The agent files use the registered names.
- Status: corrected.

## V-005 Reviewer agent smoke test

- Check: invoked both reviewer agents with a task that has a known answer. Each agent had to run `git log` and quote a line from `AGENTS.md`.
- Result: both agents ran the command and quoted the line correctly. Each reported the model from its own config file and said it could not confirm the model it runs on. The session debug log did not record model ids.
- Status: open. The user can confirm the model of each subagent call in the VS Code Chat Debug view.

## V-006 Commit convention

- AI claim: the Angular convention is the common "conventional commits" format.
- Check: fetched the Angular guidelines page instead of relying on memory.
- Result: two rules differ from the common format. The type list has no `chore`. Every commit except `docs` needs a body of at least 20 characters. Both rules are now in `AGENTS.md`. See D-011 for the earlier `chore` commit.
- Status: corrected.

M0 is finished, so I'm moving on to M1, the design doc. I'm acting as the orchestrator here, so I'm making the design decisions myself, and I'll write it to docs/design.md since it will serve as the contract the implementer subagents work from. The first section is the architecture overview, which I'm sketching as a mermaid diagram covering the Angular web app, the Fastify API with its internal components, and Postgres.

I'm settling on how to restrict the mock Slack receiver, since it runs over plain HTTP on localhost and that clashes with the HTTPS requirement. I'm leaning toward a strict URL-prefix allowlist that includes the local mock path, comparing parsed origin and path so lookalike hosts can't slip through.

Next I'm updating the security config for the mock Slack receiver: the allowlist becomes a set of URL prefixes, checked after parsing so lookalike hosts are rejected, and redirects are disabled so a webhook can't bounce the request elsewhere. The mock receiver will live as dev-only routes inside the API, and I'll rename the setting to `SLACK_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_PREFIXES` in AGENTS.md and the N4 requirement to match.

Next I'm listing the API modules under apps/api/src: the app factory for tests, the entry point that starts the server with the scheduler and worker, and config parsing. Then the database layer, auth with its guards, and the alerts, targets and sources directories, the last holding the source interface, registry, simulated feeds and scheduler.

I'm listing the remaining modules in the design: the event ingest path, which stores the event and runs the matcher in one transaction, plus pure per-category matching functions, the delivery worker with backoff, and the channel interface with email and Slack implementations. The admin and dev routes come next, with the dev routes covering event injection and the mock Slack receiver. I'm also deciding that shared schemas, including per-channel target config, belong in the common library. That still leaves open where the per-channel config schemas should sit, since adding a channel shouldn't touch core code.

I'm settling on a design for the channel UI: the target form for a new channel gets driven by a small field descriptor exported alongside its config schema in shared, so the web app doesn't need a hand-written form per channel. That means adding a channel still touches the API module, the shared schema, and the registry, and I'll say so plainly in N3 rather than pretending the UI is untouched.

Next I'm defining the target data model: the shared channel descriptor will drive the UI form generically, so adding a channel only touches the API module, the shared schema, and the registry. I'm also setting up the users table with a lowercased unique email, a password hash, and a role limited to user or admin.

I'm defining the events table now: an id, the source and category, title, summary and severity, a jsonb payload for category-specific data, and occurred and created timestamps. I'm also planning a unique constraint on source and external id so repeated real-source ingestion gets deduplicated, with the simulators setting a fresh external id for each event.

I'm defining the sources table now, with an id, category, enabled flag and updated timestamp, and keeping the polling intervals in config rather than in the table. Channels get a similar small table with an id, an enabled flag and an updated timestamp. For deliveries, I'm weighing whether deleting an alert should cascade to its delivery history, and I'm leaning toward cascade for now so the table stays simple.

I'm working out the deliveries table: a status column covering pending, sending, sent, failed, dead and skipped, with attempts, a next-attempt time, last error and sent time. A unique constraint on alert, event and target keeps each delivery to one row, and the status and next-attempt columns are indexed. I'm planning for the worker to claim due pending or failed rows in a transaction using row locks that skip locked rows.

I'm settling the delivery lease: a claimed row gets status 'sending' and a next-attempt time 60 seconds out, so a row stranded by a crash becomes claimable again after that window. That makes delivery at-least-once, so a crash after a send but before the status update could produce a duplicate message, and I'll document that plainly.

I'm setting the retry backoff as base × 2^(attempts−1) with a small jitter, injecting the random source so tests stay deterministic, and making the base configurable through an env var so the demo can use shorter delays. I'm also deciding that an admin retry resets the attempt count to zero and clears the last error, so the row gets a fresh set of tries.

I'm settling the admin retry rule: it resets the attempt count to zero, and I'm only allowing it for failed or dead deliveries. I'm leaving skipped out of retry for now since the requirement only names failed and dead. I'm also covering the case where a channel gets disabled after a delivery is already pending, so the worker marks that row skipped when it reaches it. Next is the matcher, which runs in the same transaction as the event insert, selecting enabled alerts that match the category and minimum severity, checking filters in code, and inserting delivery rows with conflicts ignored.

I'm settling the news matching rule: an event matches when any of the alert's keywords appears in its title or summary, compared case-insensitively. I'm matching on whole words rather than substrings so that "oil" won't hit "boil", and an empty keyword list will mean any news event matches.

I'm working out the per-category filter rules for market and disaster alerts, including direction, the absolute change threshold, and the earthquake-only magnitude check, and I'm about to set the severity mapping for simulated market moves.

Now I'm defining the market-move severity bands, and the earthquake magnitude bands, with news severity drawn at random from 1 to 5. Then I'm sketching the channel interface in TypeScript, where each channel gets an id, a config schema from shared, and a validate method.

I'm laying out the notification channel contract: each channel exposes a config check, an optional server-side validation step, and a send method that throws on failure. Messages get formatted once into a subject and plain text, with Slack posting the text and email using the subject and text. Slack sends go through fetch with a five-second timeout and redirects disabled, and non-2xx responses throw with the status. Email uses an SMTP transport configured from env. Next I'm sketching the event source interface.

I'm moving on to the auth section now. Registration takes an email and password, with the password needing a minimum length, and creates a user-role account and sets the session cookie. Login checks the password against the scrypt hash and sets an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie.

Now I'm settling the auth details: the JWT carries the user id and role, signed with a required secret of at least 32 characters, and logout simply clears the cookie. For admin routes, I'm going to check the user against the database on each request so that deleted users lose access, even though the role claim itself is fine since roles don't change. I'm also planning to use @fastify/jwt and @fastify/cookie, and scrypt with a 16-byte salt for password hashing.

I'm settling on the password hashing details: scrypt from node:crypto with a 16-byte salt, stored in a single combined string with its parameters, and compared with timingSafeEqual. I'm skipping native-dependency options like argon2 or bcrypt to keep the install simple. I'm also planning rate limiting on the login and register routes, and leaning on SameSite=Strict along with a JSON-only content type check for CSRF protection.

I'm now listing the API routes, starting with the auth endpoints for register, login, logout, and fetching the current user. Then I'm moving on to the user-facing target routes, where I'm sketching how to list, create, and delete a target.

I'm laying out the alert endpoints next: the targets section ends with a test route that sends a notification right away, outside the queue, and returns success or an error. For alerts I'm listing list, create, fetch, replace, and delete, plus a PATCH to toggle enabled, with every query scoped to the owning user and a 404 for anything that belongs to someone else.

Next I'm listing the admin endpoints: users with their alert counts, a user's alerts, and a paginated event feed filtered by category and limit with a created-at cursor.

I'm settling the admin endpoints for deliveries, sources, channels, and metrics, with each list taking filters and a before cursor. For metrics, I'm defining the failure rate per channel as dead deliveries over sent plus dead within the last 24 hours.

Now I'm listing the dev-only endpoints, which are only available outside production. There's an event ingest route that runs through the same path as the real sources, a mock Slack receiver that records messages and can be switched into a failure mode to return 500s, plus routes to read and clear the recorded messages.

I'm settling the dev-only details: the Slack channel will post to a mock receiver on localhost under the dev path, and that prefix gets allowlisted only outside production, with the default Slack prefix still in place. For pagination I'm using a limit defaulting to 50 and capped at 200, plus a timestamp cursor. I'm keeping Fastify's default error shape rather than a custom one to save time.

Now I'm laying out the web app section: an Angular 22 app using standalone components and signals, with whatever defaults the generator produces, and a dev proxy that sends /api to the backend on port 3000 so the cookie stays same-origin. The routes cover login and register, the alerts list, new alert, and alert detail pages, targets, and the admin pages for users, events, deliveries, settings with sources and channels, and metrics, all guarded by an auth guard.

I'm going to cover the web app's frontend guards, alert form, and admin refresh behavior. I'm also listing the Spartan UI components I need and checking which ones exist in version 1.10. Last, I'm writing out the env file with the database URL, JWT secret, and SMTP settings.

I'm listing the remaining env settings: the alert email sender address, the Slack prefixes that include the local mock path, the delivery backoff and retry limits, the worker poll interval, the source polling bounds, the seed accounts for admin and user, and the port.

I'm noting the remaining environment settings, then moving on to the testing plan: unit tests for matching, severity, backoff, the Slack allowlist, and password hashing, and integration tests against a real Postgres database covering auth, ownership, admin access, and the full event-to-delivery path.

I'm going through the end-to-end Playwright scenario next, where the demo user creates a Slack target and an alert, and the event is injected through the API and checked via the mock Slack messages. # Design This document is the contract between the implementer subagents. Requirement ids such as R9 refer to `docs/requirements.md`. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Browser Web[Angular 22 app
port 4200] end subgraph API[Fastify API, port 3000] Routes[HTTP routes] Sched[Source scheduler] Ingest[Ingest and match] Worker[Delivery worker] Reg[Channel registry] Mock[Mock Slack receiver
dev only] end PG[(PostgreSQL 18)] Mailpit[Mailpit
SMTP 1025, UI 8025] Web -- "/api via dev proxy" --> Routes Sched --> Ingest Routes -- "/api/dev/events" --> Ingest Ingest --> PG Worker --> PG Worker --> Reg Reg -- email --> Mailpit Reg -- slack --> Mock ``` One API process runs the HTTP server, the source scheduler and the delivery worker. The Angular dev server proxies `/api` to the API, so the browser sees one origin and the auth cookie works without CORS. ## Event flow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant S as Source or /api/dev/events participant I as ingestEvent participant DB as PostgreSQL participant W as Worker participant C as Channel S->>I: NewEvent I->>DB: BEGIN, insert event I->>DB: select enabled alerts where category matches and min_severity <= severity I->>I: matchesFilters(event, alert) for each alert I->>DB: insert deliveries ... on conflict do nothing I->>DB: COMMIT loop every WORKER_POLL_MS W->>DB: claim up to 10 due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED W->>C: send(config, message) alt success W->>DB: status = sent else error, attempts < max W->>DB: status = failed, next_attempt_at = now + backoff else error, attempts = max W->>DB: status = dead end end ``` Filter matching runs in TypeScript, not SQL. The SQL query only narrows by category, `enabled` and `min_severity`. This keeps every filter rule in one pure function with unit tests. ## Repository layout ```text apps/ api/src/ main.ts starts the server, scheduler and worker app.ts buildApp(config) for tests and main config.ts reads env with zod db/ schema.ts, client.ts, migrations/, seed.ts auth/ routes, password.ts, plugin with requireUser and requireAdmin targets/ routes, service alerts/ routes, service events/ ingest.ts matching/ match.ts, severity.ts delivery/ worker.ts, backoff.ts, message.ts channels/ channel.ts, registry.ts, email.ts, slack.ts, slack-url.ts sources/ source.ts, registry.ts, scheduler.ts, simulated/{news,market,disaster}.ts admin/ routes dev/ routes for event injection and the mock Slack receiver web/src/app/ core/ api client, auth store, guards auth/ login and register pages alerts/ list and form targets/ list and form admin/ users, events, deliveries, settings, metrics web-e2e/ Playwright libs/ shared/src/ zod schemas, types, channel descriptors docker-compose.yml .env.example ``` ## Shared library `libs/shared` holds every type that crosses the HTTP boundary, as zod schemas with inferred TypeScript types. Both apps import from it. - `Category = 'news' | 'market' | 'disaster'` - `Region = 'africa' | 'asia' | 'europe' | 'north-america' | 'south-america' | 'oceania'` - `Severity`: integer from 1 to 5 - `EventData`: a discriminated union on `category` - news: `{}`. The text is in `title` and `summary`. - market: `{ symbol: string, price: number, changePct: number }`. `changePct` is signed. - disaster: `{ type: 'earthquake' | 'flood' | 'storm' | 'wildfire', region: Region, magnitude?: number }` - `AlertFilters`: a discriminated union on `category` - news: `{ keywords: string[] }` - market: `{ symbols: string[], direction: 'up' | 'down' | 'any', minChangePct: number }` - disaster: `{ types: DisasterType[], regions: Region[], minMagnitude?: number }` - `TargetConfig` per channel - email: `{ address: string }` - slack: `{ webhookUrl: string }` - `channelDescriptors`: for each channel, a label and a list of form fields `{ key, label, inputType }`. The web app builds the target form from this list, so a new channel needs no new form component. - Request and response DTOs for every route below. ## Data model All ids are UUIDs except `sources.id` and `channels.id`. All timestamps are `timestamptz` in UTC. | Table | Columns | Constraints and indexes | |---|---|---| | `users` | id, email, password_hash, role, created_at | email unique, stored lowercase. role in (`user`, `admin`) | | `targets` | id, user_id, name, channel, config jsonb, created_at | user_id references users on delete cascade | | `alerts` | id, user_id, name, category, filters jsonb, min_severity, enabled, created_at, updated_at | user_id references users on delete cascade. min_severity between 1 and 5 | | `alert_targets` | alert_id, target_id | primary key on both. Both reference their tables on delete cascade | | `events` | id, source_id, external_id, category, title, summary, severity, data jsonb, occurred_at, created_at | unique (source_id, external_id). Index (category, created_at desc) | | `sources` | id, category, enabled, updated_at | Seeded rows: `news-sim`, `market-sim`, `disaster-sim` | | `channels` | id, enabled, updated_at | Seeded rows: `email`, `slack` | | `deliveries` | id, alert_id, event_id, target_id, channel, status, attempts, next_attempt_at, last_error, sent_at, created_at, updated_at | unique (alert_id, event_id, target_id) for R9. Index (status, next_attempt_at) | `events.external_id` lets a future real source skip events it has already stored. Simulators set it to a random UUID. `deliveries.channel` is copied from the target when the row is created, so metrics per channel need no join. ### Delivery states ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> pending: channel enabled [*] --> skipped: channel disabled (R11) pending --> sending: worker claims failed --> sending: worker claims after next_attempt_at sending --> sent: send ok sending --> failed: error and attempts < max sending --> dead: error and attempts = max sending --> sending: lease expired, claimed again pending --> skipped: channel disabled before send failed --> pending: admin retry dead --> pending: admin retry ``` - Claim query: rows with status `pending` or `failed` and `next_attempt_at <= now()`, plus rows with status `sending` whose lease has expired. The claim sets status `sending`, increments `attempts`, and sets `next_attempt_at = now() + 60s` as a lease. A worker that crashes mid-send leaves the row to be claimed again after 60 seconds. - Delivery is therefore at least once. A crash after a successful send and before the status update sends the message a second time. This is acceptable for alerts. - Backoff after failed attempt n: `DELIVERY_BACKOFF_BASE_MS * 2^(n-1)`, plus up to 10% random jitter. With the default base of 30 seconds, the waits are 30 s, 60 s, 120 s and 240 s. The fifth failure sets `dead`. `computeBackoff(attempt, baseMs, random)` takes `random` as an argument so tests are deterministic. - Admin retry (R14) is allowed only from `failed` or `dead`. It sets status `pending`, `attempts = 0`, `next_attempt_at = now()` and clears `last_error`. - When the worker claims a row whose channel is disabled, it sets `skipped` without sending. ## Matching rules `matchesFilters(event, alert)` returns true only when the event category equals the alert category, `event.severity >= alert.minSeverity`, and the category rule below holds. | Category | Rule | |---|---| | news | `keywords` is empty, or at least one keyword appears in the title or summary as a whole word, case-insensitive. Keywords are regex-escaped before use. | | market | `symbols` is empty or contains the event symbol, compared in uppercase. `direction` is `any`, or `up` with `changePct > 0`, or `down` with `changePct < 0`. `abs(changePct) >= minChangePct`. | | disaster | `types` is empty or contains the event type. `regions` is empty or contains the event region. If `minMagnitude` is set and the event is an earthquake, `magnitude >= minMagnitude`. `minMagnitude` is ignored for other types. | ### Severity for simulated events | Category | Severity | |---|---| | market | from `abs(changePct)`: below 2 is 1, below 5 is 2, below 10 is 3, below 20 is 4, otherwise 5 | | disaster, earthquake | from magnitude: below 5 is 1, below 6 is 2, below 7 is 3, below 8 is 4, otherwise 5 | | disaster, other types | random from 1 to 5 | | news | random from 1 to 5. Titles of severity 4 and 5 start with "Breaking:" | Simulated market moves are mostly small, so high severity is rare on the timer. Demos use `/api/dev/events` to get a specific event. ## Extension points ### Channels ```ts interface NotificationChannel { readonly id: ChannelId; readonly configSchema: ZodType; // Extra server-side checks, such as the Slack URL allowlist. Throws on invalid config. assertConfigAllowed?(config: C): void; // Throws on failure. The worker records the error message. send(config: C, message: NotificationMessage): Promise; } interface NotificationMessage { subject: string; text: string; } ``` `delivery/message.ts` builds one `NotificationMessage` from an event and an alert. Email sends `subject` and `text`. Slack posts `{ "text": "**\n" }`. To add a channel: 1. Add its config schema and descriptor in `libs/shared`. 2. Add a class in `apps/api/src/channels/` that implements `NotificationChannel`. 3. Register it in `channels/registry.ts` and add a row to the `channels` table in the seed. ### Sources ```ts interface EventSource { readonly id: string; readonly category: Category; // Delay before the next poll. nextDelayMs(): number; poll(): Promise; } ``` The scheduler keeps one `setTimeout` chain per registered source. Before each poll it reads `sources.enabled` from the database and skips the poll if the source is disabled (R15). Each simulator returns one event per poll and a delay between `SOURCE_MIN_INTERVAL_MS` and `SOURCE_MAX_INTERVAL_MS` (R7). A real source, such as the USGS feed, would return many events per poll and rely on `external_id` to skip repeats. ## Security | Concern | Measure | |---|---| | Password storage | `node:crypto` scrypt with a 16-byte random salt. Stored as `scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash`. Compared with `timingSafeEqual`. No native module is needed. | | Session | JWT signed with HS256 and `JWT_SECRET`, which must be at least 32 characters. Claims are `sub` and `role`. Expiry is 8 hours. Sent in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie, with `Secure` in production. | | CSRF | `SameSite=Strict` stops browsers from sending the cookie on cross-site requests. Mutating routes accept only `application/json`. | | Authorization | `requireUser` verifies the JWT and loads the user from the database, so a deleted user loses access at once. `requireAdmin` also checks `role = 'admin'`. Every admin route uses `requireAdmin`. | | Object access | Every target and alert query filters by `user_id`. A request for another user's object returns 404. Alert `targetIds` must belong to the same user. | | Brute force | `@fastify/rate-limit` on `/api/auth/login` and `/api/auth/register`: 10 requests per minute per IP. | | Input validation | Every body, query and params object is validated with the shared zod schemas. ## D-015 Passwords hashed with scrypt from `node:crypto`

- Options: argon2, bcrypt, bcryptjs, scrypt from `node:crypto`.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: argon2 and bcrypt need native builds, which can break on a new Node major. bcryptjs is slow pure JavaScript. scrypt is built into Node and is memory-hard.

## D-016 JWT in an HttpOnly cookie, same origin through the dev proxy

- Options: bearer token in `localStorage`, HttpOnly cookie.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: a script injected through XSS cannot read an HttpOnly cookie. The Angular dev proxy serves the API on the same origin, so `SameSite=Strict` works and CORS is not needed.

## D-017 Filter matching in TypeScript

- Options: translate filters to SQL, load candidate alerts and match in TypeScript.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: one pure function holds every rule and gets table-driven unit tests. SQL narrows by category, enabled flag and minimum severity first. The limit on alert count is listed in `docs/design.md`.

## D-018 At-least-once delivery with a 60 second lease

- Options: at most once, at least once with a lease.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: a lost alert is worse than a repeated one. The lease lets another worker pick up a row after a crash.

## D-019 Slack URL allowlist by prefix

- Options: host allowlist, URL prefix allowlist, resolve DNS and block private IP ranges.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: a prefix such as `https://hooks.slack.com/services/` fixes scheme, host and path in one rule. Development adds the mock receiver's prefix. Redirects are refused, so an allowed URL cannot forward the request elsewhere.

## D-020 Channel descriptors drive the target form

- Options: one Angular form component per channel, a generic form built from a field list in `libs/shared`.
- Decided by: orchestrator.
- Reason: requirement N3 asks that a new channel need no changes outside its own module. A field list keeps the web app out of that change.

Crash walk-through: claim 5 sets attempts=5, the process crashes, and 60 s later a reclaim sets attempts=6 and sends a sixth time. That breaks R10.     13[2C| Event | One thing that happened in the world, such as an earthquake or a 7% drop in a stock price. It has a category, a severity from 1 to 5, and category-specific data. |
    14[2C| Category | `news`, `market` or `disaster` |

    22
    23[2C## Functional requirements
    24
    25[2C### Users
    26

    35[2C- R6. Every alert has a minimum severity from 1 to 5.
    36
    37[2C### System
    38
    39[2C- R7. Each enabled source produces one event at a random interval between 20 and 60 seconds.
    40[2C- R8. When an event is stored, the system evaluates it against every enabled alert in the same category.
    41[2C- R9. For each match, the system creates one delivery per target. The same alert, event and target never produce a second delivery.
    42[2C- R10. A worker sends pending deliveries. A failed send is retried with exponential backoff, up to 5 attempts in total. After the fifth failure the delivery is marked `dead`.
    43[2C- R11. If an admin has disabled a channel, new deliveries for that channel are stored with status `skipped`, so the admin can see why nothing was sent.

    48[2C- R13. An admin can browse stored events and filter them by category.

response.value:
I'm weighing both reviews, and they agree on two problems. Attempts aren't capped when a job is reclaimed, which can lead to a sixth send. The lease is also shorter than the SMTP timeouts, which can cause duplicate sends. I'll accept both fixes: set send timeouts, raise the lease to 60s, and send each batch concurrently with Promise.allSettled.

I'm settling on the fixes from both reviews: the completion update gets guarded by the claimed attempts value so a stale worker can't overwrite a newer claim. For the disabled-channel case, I'm leaning toward letting queued rows wait while a channel is off, and only creating new rows as skipped when they arrive during that window.

I'm working through the remaining review items: the disabled-channel rows should stay queued and resume when the channel is re-enabled, while new arrivals get stored as skipped, and I'm considering letting admins retry skipped rows too. I'm also making the channel and source seeds upsert from the registries at startup, and weighing how to reject the placeholder JWT secret without breaking the one-command local setup.

I'm making sure each Slack webhook prefix is a valid URL ending in a slash, rejecting credentials in the URL, and allowing plain http only outside production. I'll also make sure error messages never include the webhook URL, so the admin API only exposes the target name.

I'm accepting the remaining review items: the rate limit becomes a config value that tests can raise, the out-of-scope wording gets reworded around notification rate limiting, and I'm dropping the `before` cursors so pagination is `limit` only. I'm also removing the text/plain parser, and I'm checking whether a SameSite cookie alone covers bodyless mutations, since a sibling subdomain would still count as same-site.

I'm deciding the FK behavior: deliveries cascade when their alert or target is deleted, so a deleted alert's history goes away, which I'll document. Defaults go on attempts and next_attempt_at so they're never null. Deleting a target in use is fine since its deliveries cascade with it, and the source_id of 'dev' has no matching row, which I still need to handle.

I'm adopting the reviewers' suggestion to switch the regex matching to lookarounds with the `u` flag, so keywords like C++ and $TSLA match correctly, and moving empty-keyword handling into the R5 rule. For the stack, I'm going with node-postgres via drizzle, drizzle-kit for migrations, and npm scripts for setup and dev.

I'm deciding a few last details: a missing magnitude will simply fail a minimum-magnitude check, and test sends will be refused with a 409 when the channel is disabled. Admin retries will use a conditional update that only matches rows in a retryable status, returning 409 if nothing matches, and the scheduler will pick a fresh random delay each time.

I'm going to have the integration tests start the app on a real port, since `.inject` won't reach a mock Slack endpoint, and point the Slack allowlist at that port. I'll also define the mock's body as `{ text: string }` so it matches the shared schema, and document that a logout doesn't revoke a JWT until it expires.

I'm rejecting the proposed scope cut on the PATCH route, since enabling or disabling an alert from the list needs it and it's trivial to keep. For the user view, I'll simplify it to a users table with an alert count, where selecting a user shows their alerts. I'm also keeping the separate test database rather than truncating the dev one, since a one-line createdb in the compose init script is cheap insurance against wiping dev data.

I'm checking the remaining review points: the admin's auth check should read the user's role from the database rather than trusting the JWT claim. I'm also keeping a few items deferred or rejected, such as the Origin check, the PATCH route cut, and truncating the dev database.

edits.text:
claim
  failed --> sending: claim after next_attempt_at
  sending --> sending: lease expired and attempts < max, claimed again
  sending --> dead: lease expired and attempts >= max
  sending --> sent: send ok
  sending --> failed: error and attempts < max
  sending --> dead: error and attempts >= max
  failed --> pending: admin retry
  dead --> pending: admin retry
  skipped --> pending: admin retry
```

- Ingest creates a row as `skipped`, with `attempts = 0` and `last_error = 'channel disabled'`, when its channel is disabled. Otherwise the row starts as `pending`.
- The claim is one statement, `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10) RETURNING *`, and it commits before any send starts. It picks rows that meet all of these conditions:
  - the row's channel is enabled
  - `attempts < DELIVERY_MAX_ATTEMPTS`
  - status is `pending` or `failed` with `next_attempt_at <= now()`, or status is `sending` with an expired lease, meaning `next_attempt_at <= now()`
- The claim sets status `sending`, increments `attempts`, and sets `next_attempt_at = now() + DELIVERY_LEASE_MS` as a lease.
- Before each claim, one more statement sets `dead` on every `sending` row whose lease has expired and whose `attempts >= DELIVERY_MAX_ATTEMPTS`. A crash during the last attempt therefore never leads to an extra send.
- Rows whose channel is disabled after they were created keep their status. The claim ignores them until the admin enables the channel again.
- The worker sends all claimed rows at the same time with `Promise.allSettled`. Each send has a deadline well below the 60 second lease. Slack uses a 5 second `AbortSignal.timeout`. Nodemailer uses `connectionTimeout`, `greetingTimeout` and `socketTimeout` of 10 seconds each. The Nodemailer defaults run up to 10 minutes, which would outlive the lease.
- Every result update is fenced with `WHERE id = :id AND status = 'sending' AND attempts = :claimedAttempts`. If no row matches, a newer claim owns the row and the worker drops the stale result.
- The next poll is scheduled with `setTimeout` after the batch finishes, so polls never overlap.
- Delivery is at least once. A crash after a successful send and before the result update sends the message again on the next claim. A lost alert is worse than a repeated one.
- Backoff after failed attempt n: `DELIVERY_BACKOFF_BASE_MS * 2^(n-1)`, plus up to 10% random jitter. With the default base of 30 seconds, the waits are 30 s, 60 s, 120 s and 240 s. The fifth failure sets `dead`. `computeBackoff(attempt, baseMs, random)` takes `random` as an argument so tests are deterministic.
- Admin retry (R14) is one conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND status IN ('failed', 'dead', 'skipped') RETURNING id`. It sets status `pending`, `attempts = 0`, `next_attempt_at = now()` and clears `last_error`. If no row comes back, the route returns 409.
- `last_error` holds a short message such as `Slack responded 500` or `SMTP timeout`. It never contains the webhook URL or SMTP credentials

. `source_id` has no foreign key, so injected events can use `dev` |
| `sources` | id, category, enabled, updated_at | Rows come from the source registry at startup |
| `channels` | id, enabled, updated_at | Rows come from the channel registry at startup |
| `deliveries` | id, alert_id, event_id, target_id, channel, status, attempts, next_attempt_at, last_error, sent_at, created_at, updated_at | unique (alert_id, event_id, target_id) for R9. alert_id, event_id and target_id reference their tables on delete cascade. `attempts` not null default 0. `next_attempt_at` not null default now(). Index (status, next_attempt_at) |

At startup the API inserts a `sources` row for each registered source and a `channels` row for each registered channel, with `enabled = true`, using `on conflict do nothing`. A restart never overwrites a switch the admin has set.

{"content": "# AGENTS.md

Instructions for every AI agent working in this repository.

## Project

An alerting app. Users create alert rules for world events in three categories: news, market and disaster. When an event matches a rule, the app notifies the user by email or Slack. Admins see all users, alerts, events and deliveries.

The repository is an interview submission. Reviewers grade the process, so the process artifacts matter as much as the code.

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/plan.md` | Milestones, order, cut list |
| `docs/requirements.md` | How the brief was interpreted, assumptions, out of scope |
| `docs/design.md` | Architecture, data model, API |
| `docs/decision-log.md` | Decisions with options and reasons |
| `docs/ai-review-log.md` | AI output that was checked, rejected or corrected |
| `prompts/prompt-log.md` | User prompts, word for word |
| `prompts/subagents/` | Prompts the orchestrator sent to subagents |

Read `docs/requirements.md` and `docs/design.md` before changing code.

## Stack

- Node.js 26 LTS, TypeScript, npm
- Nx 24 monorepo: `apps/api`, `apps/web`, `libs/shared`
- Backend: Fastify 5, Drizzle ORM, PostgreSQL 18
- Frontend: Angular 22, spartan-ng with Tailwind 4
- Email: Nodemailer to Mailpit. Slack: incoming webhook, with a mock receiver in development
- Docker Compose runs Postgres and Mailpit

## Agent roles

| Role | Who | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | Main chat agent | Plans, writes subagent prompts, verifies output, reconciles reviews, commits |
| Implementer | Default subagent | Writes code for one scoped task from a saved prompt |
| Explorer | `Explore` subagent | Read-only lookups |
| Reviewer A | `reviewer-opus` on Claude Opus 5.5 | Independent read-only review |
| Reviewer B | `reviewer-gpt` on GPT-6.2 Sol | Independent read-only review |

The two reviewer files in `.github/agents/` share the same body. Only the model differs. Keep the bodies identical so the reviews are comparable.

## Milestone workflow

1. The orchestrator saves the subagent prompt to `prompts/subagents/NNN-<slug>.md` before sending it.
2. An implementer subagent does the task.
3. The orchestrator checks the result itself: reads the diff, runs build and tests, and checks package versions with `npm view`.
4. Both reviewers get the same review prompt and run in parallel.
5. The orchestrator compares the two reviews. It accepts, rejects or defers each finding and records the outcome with a reason in `docs/ai-review-log.md`.
6. The orchestrator commits. The user pushes. Agents never push.

## Commit messages

Follow the [Angular commit message guidelines](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/main/contributing-docs/commit-message-guidelines.md).

```text
<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

<body>

<footer>
```

- Type is one of `build`, `ci`, `docs`, `feat`, `fix`, `perf`, `refactor`, `test`.
- Scope is optional. Use `api`, `web`, `shared`, `e2e` or `infra`. Leave the scope empty for repository-wide docs.
- Write the summary in the imperative present tense, start it with a lowercase letter, and leave out the final period.
- Every commit except `docs` needs a body of at least 20 characters that explains why.

## Writing rules

Apply `.agents/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` to all prose in `docs/`, `prompts/`, `README.md` and this file.

## Code rules

- Keep secrets out of git. Put defaults in `.env.example`.
- The API rejects Slack webhook URLs whose host is not on the allowlist in `SLACK_WEBHOOK_ALLOWED_HOSTS`.
- Routes under `/dev` are registered only when `NODE_ENV` is not `production`.
- Validate every request body with the zod schemas in `libs/shared`.

{"content": "# Plan

## Goal

Turn a one-paragraph product brief into a working alerting app and record how the work was done. The graders read the process artifacts first and use the code as evidence for them.

## Constraints

- About 2.5 hours on day one. The user may continue on day two.
- One developer directs AI agents. The orchestrator agent delegates implementation to subagents and sends every milestone to two reviewer agents on different models.
- Local run only.

## Deliverables

| Deliverable | Path | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | `docs/plan.md` | Shows scope, order and the cut list |
| Requirements | `docs/requirements.md` | Turns the vague brief into testable statements and lists assumptions |
| Design | `docs/design.md` | Fixes the data model and API before any code, so subagents share one contract |
| Decision log | `docs/decision-log.md` | Records each choice with the options and the reason |
| AI review log | `docs/ai-review-log.md` | Records what AI output was checked, rejected or corrected |
| Prompt history | `prompts/` | User prompts word for word, subagent prompts, chat exports |
| Agent setup | `AGENTS.md`, `.github/agents/` | Shows how the agents were directed |
| Code | `apps/`, `libs/`, `docker-compose.yml` | Evidence that the design works |
| README | `README.md` | Run instructions, demo script, screenshots |

## Milestones

Each milestone ends with a commit that follows the Angular convention in `AGENTS.md`.

| ID | Milestone | Budget | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0 | Process docs, agent setup, prompt log | 10 min | Files committed |
| M1 | Design doc, reviewed by both reviewer agents | 15 min | The user approves the data model and API list |
| M2 | Nx workspace, Docker Compose, shared library | 15 min | `nx run-many -t build` passes and the containers start |
| M3 | Backend: schema, seed, auth, CRUD, generators, matcher, worker, both channels, unit tests | 40 min | An injected event produces an email in Mailpit and a message in the mock Slack receiver |
| M4 | Frontend: user pages and admin pages | 35 min | The demo script in the README works by hand |
| M5 | API integration tests and one Playwright smoke test | 15 min | All tests pass |
| M6 | README, screenshots, final review log, chat export | 15 min | Submission is ready to push |

## Order and reasons

1. Process docs come first. The graders read them first, and every later subagent prompt points at them.
2. The design comes before code. Implementer subagents run in isolated contexts, so the design doc is the only contract they share.
3. The backend comes before the frontend. Matching, dedup and retries carry the most risk, and the UI only displays their results.
4. Tests run alongside the backend work. The matcher and the retry timing get unit tests in M3, and M5 adds the integration tests and the end-to-end test.

## Cut list

If a milestone runs over budget, features are cut in this order:

1. Metrics page
2. Playwright smoke test
3. Admin switches for sources and channels

The process docs are never cut.

## Day two candidates

These items are out of scope for day one. They come back if time allows:

- Rate limiting and digest batching
- Quiet hours
- A real event source, such as the USGS earthquake feed
- A third channel to prove the extension point

{"content": "# Requirements

## The brief

> We want users to be able to set up alerts so they get notified when something important happens in the world, like breaking news, market movements, natural disasters, that kind of thing. Should work for both email and Slack. Make it flexible enough that we can add more channels later. We need an admin view too.

No product manager is available, so the user acts as the product owner. Answers are in `prompts/prompt-log.md`, entries 002 and 003.

## Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Event | One thing that happened in the world, such as an earthquake or a 7% drop in a stock price. It has a category, a severity from 1 to 5, and category-specific data. |
| Category | `news`, `market` or `disaster` |
| Source | A component that produces events for one category. On day one, every source is a simulator. |
| Alert | A rule owned by a user: a category, typed filters, a minimum severity, and one or more targets |
| Target | A destination owned by a user, such as an email address or a Slack webhook URL |
| Channel | A delivery mechanism, `email` or `slack`. Each target uses one channel. |
| Delivery | One attempt record for sending one event to one target because of one alert |

"Something important" means an event that matches an alert's filters and has a severity at or above the alert's minimum severity.

## Functional requirements

### Users

- R1. A visitor can register and sign in with an email address and a password.
- R2. A user can create, list and delete targets. An email target has an address. A Slack target has an incoming webhook URL.
- R3. A user can send a test notification to a target.
- R4. A user can create, edit, delete, enable and disable alerts.
- R5. Alert filters depend on the category:
  - news: keywords matched against the title and summary, case-insensitive, any keyword matches
  - market: symbols (an empty list means any symbol), direction (`up`, `down`, `any`), minimum absolute change in percent
  - disaster: types (`earthquake`, `flood`, `storm`, `wildfire`; an empty list means any type), regions (an empty list means any region), minimum magnitude for earthquakes
- R6. Every alert has a minimum severity from 1 to 5.

### System

- R7. Each enabled source produces one event at a random interval between 20 and 60 seconds.
- R8. When an event is stored, the system evaluates it against every enabled alert in the same category.
- R9. For each match, the system creates one delivery per target. The same alert, event and target never produce a second delivery.
- R10. A worker sends pending deliveries. A failed send is retried with exponential backoff, up to 5 attempts in total. After the fifth failure the delivery is marked `dead`.
- R11. If an admin has disabled a channel, new deliveries for that channel are stored with status `skipped`, so the admin can see why nothing was sent.

### Admin

- R12. An admin can list all users and the alerts each user owns.
- R13. An admin can browse stored events and filter them by category.
- R14. An admin can browse deliveries, filter them by status and channel, and retry a `failed` or `dead` delivery.
- R15. An admin can enable and disable each source and each channel.
- R16. An admin can see metrics for the last 24 hours: events per category, deliveries per status, and failure rate per channel.

### Development and demo

- R17. A route that exists only outside production lets a developer inject a specific event. Tests and demos use it to get predictable results.
- R18. A mock Slack receiver records incoming webhook calls and can be set to fail, so retries can be shown without a Slack workspace.

## Non-functional requirements

- N1. One command starts the stack locally after `docker compose up -d`. A seed script creates one admin and one demo user.
- N2. Passwords are stored as salted hashes. Admin routes check the role on the server.
- N3. Adding a channel needs one new module that implements the channel interface, one config schema, and one registry entry. The same applies to adding a source.
- N4. Slack webhook URLs must use HTTPS and a host from an allowlist. Development adds the mock receiver's host to the allowlist.
- N5. Unit tests cover filter matching, severity checks and backoff timing. Integration tests cover the API. One Playwright test covers sign-in, alert creation and delivery.

## Assumptions

- A1. Simulated events are enough to show the design. Real sources plug into the same source interface later.
- A2. A single API process runs the generators and the worker. The worker claims rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so a second process would not send twice.
- A3. All times are stored in UTC.
- A4. The UI is in English.

## Out of scope for day one

- Real data sources
- Rate limiting, digest batching and quiet hours
- Email verification and password reset
- Channels other than email and Slack
- Organisations or teams
- Deployment
